stem: The polynomial function R(x) = (1 − x²)(x² + 4) is written as a product of two factors. Which statement describes its end behavior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The graph rises on the left and falls on the right

choices.label: B
choices.text: The graph rises on both the left and the right

choices.label: C
choices.text: The graph falls on the left and rises on the right

choices.label: D
choices.text: The graph falls on both the left and the right

rationales.A: Describes an odd-degree polynomial with a negative leading coefficient (rises left, falls right). R has even degree 4, so both ends point the same direction, and the leading term is -x^4, so both ends fall.
rationales.B: Reads the factor 1 − x² as if its leading term were +x², obtaining x²·x² = x⁴ with a positive coefficient; the leading term is actually −x².
rationales.C: Treats the function as odd-degree. Expanding gives R(x) = −x⁴ − 3x² + 4, whose degree is 4 (even), so the ends point the same direction.
rationales.D: Multiplying leading terms gives (−x²)(x²) = −x⁴, so R has even degree 4 and a negative leading coefficient (R(x) = −x⁴ − 3x² + 4); both ends fall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 ln 7

rationales.A: Drops the factor 2, treating the equation as e^(3x) = 14, so 3x = ln 14. Check: x = (ln 14)/3 gives 2e^(ln 14) = 28, not 14.
rationales.B: Multiplies ln 7 by 3 instead of dividing by 3 when solving 3x = ln 7.
rationales.C: Divide by 2 first: e^(3x) = 7. Then 3x = ln 7, so x = (ln 7)/3.
rationales.D: Removes the 3 by dividing the argument, giving ln(7/3); the 3 multiplies x in the exponent and must come out as a divisor of ln 7.

stem: On the interval 0 ≤ x < 2π, which gives all solutions of 2sin x + 1 = 0?

choices.label: A
choices.text: π/6 and 5π/6

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5π/6 and 7π/6

choices.label: C
choices.text: 7π/6 and 11π/6

choices.label: D
choices.text: 7π/6 only

rationales.A: These are the solutions of sin x = +1/2. The sign was lost when moving the 1 to the other side.
rationales.B: Pairs 7*pi/6, which is a solution of sin x = -1/2, with 5*pi/6, which is a solution of sin x = +1/2. Check: sin(5*pi/6) = +1/2, so 2 sin x + 1 = 2, not 0, and 5*pi/6 is not a solution. It also omits 11*pi/6.
rationales.C: sin x = −1/2. Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV, where the reference angle π/6 gives x = π + π/6 = 7π/6 and x = 2π − π/6 = 11π/6.
rationales.D: Finds the Quadrant III solution but omits the Quadrant IV solution, 11π/6, where sine is also −1/2.

The polynomial q(x) = x⁴ − 13x² + 36 has which complete set of real zeros?

rationales.A: Uses u = 4 and u = 9 (values of x^2) and their negatives as if they were values of x. The values 4 and 9 are solutions for x^2, not x; check: q(4) = 256 - 208 + 36 = 84, not 0.
rationales.B: Let u = x². Then u² − 13u + 36 = (u − 4)(u − 9) = 0, so x² = 4 or x² = 9, giving x = ±2 and x = ±3.
rationales.C: Takes only the positive square roots of x² = 4 and x² = 9, omitting −2 and −3.
rationales.D: Omits the positive root +3 from x² = 9.

Find all x satisfying (9−x)/(x+8)≥0.

rationales.A: The interval is right, but the inequality is nonstrict, so x=9, where the quotient equals 0, must be included.
rationales.B: The interval is right, but x=−8 makes the denominator 0, so the expression is undefined there and −8 must be excluded.
rationales.C: This is the solution set of (x-9)/(x+8) >= 0, with the numerator sign reversed. For (9-x)/(x+8), values with x < -8 or x > 9 give negative quotients (x = 10 gives -1/18, x = -9 gives -18). Only the single value x = 9 (quotient 0) works there, and the interval (-8, 9), where the quotient is positive, is missing.
rationales.D: The critical values are x=9 (quotient 0, included) and x=−8 (undefined, excluded). For −8<x<9 both 9−x and x+8 are positive, so the quotient is positive; for x<−8 and x>9 it is negative.

For x=0, 1, 2, 3, 4, a quantity has values 80, 60.4, 45.1, 34.2, 25.6. Which claim is best supported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A quadratic model, because the second differences are exactly constant

choices.label: B
choices.text: An exponential decay model, because successive ratios are near 0.75

choices.label: C
choices.text: A linear model, because a linear regression has r² greater than 0.95

choices.label: D
choices.text: An exponential growth model, because the outputs are multiplied by about 1.33 each step

rationales.A: The first differences are −19.6, −15.3, −10.9, −8.6, and the second differences are 4.3, 4.4, 2.3, which are not constant.
rationales.B: The ratios of each value to the previous one are about 0.755, 0.747, 0.758, 0.749, nearly constant near 0.75, which indicates exponential decay.
rationales.C: A linear fit does have r^2 = 0.973, but a high r^2 alone does not show that a linear model is the best description. The first differences are -19.6, -15.3, -10.9, -8.6, which are not constant (linear data would have constant differences), while the successive ratios are all near 0.75, so an exponential model is better supported.
rationales.D: 1.33 is about 1/0.75, the ratio of a value to the next one. Going from one value to the next multiplies by about 0.75, which is less than 1, so the model is decay, not growth.

A population model is P(t)=12e^(0.07t), where t is in years. At what time t is P(t)=50, to the nearest tenth?

rationales.A: Finds 50/12 correctly but undoes the exponential e^( ) with log₁₀ instead of ln: log₁₀(50/12)/0.07≈8.9.
rationales.B: Takes the log of both sides without handling the factor 12, writing 0.07t = ln 50, so t = ln(50)/0.07 = 55.9. But ln(12e^(0.07t)) = ln 12 + 0.07t, so the 12 must be divided out first. Check: P(55.9) = 12e^(3.913) is about 600, not 50.
rationales.C: Subtracts 12 instead of dividing by it: 0.07t=ln(38)≈3.638, so t≈52.0.

A model is y=7.5−2.4ln(x). What x gives y=3, to the nearest tenth?

rationales.B: Makes two sign errors: adds 7.5 instead of subtracting it and also drops the negative sign on -2.4, giving ln(x) = (3 + 7.5)/2.4 = 4.375 and x = e^4.375, about 79.4.
rationales.C: Divides by 2.4 but loses the sign of the coefficient: ln(x)=(3−7.5)/2.4=−1.875, so x=e^(−1.875)≈0.153, or 0.2.
rationales.D: Ignores the constant 7.5 and also drops the negative sign on -2.4, giving ln(x) = 3/2.4 = 1.25 and x = e^1.25, about 3.5.

stem: As x approaches positive infinity, what is the end behavior of f(x) = 100x^3 − 5x^4 + x^2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: f(x) approaches positive infinity

choices.label: B
choices.text: f(x) approaches 0

choices.label: C
choices.text: f(x) approaches −5

choices.label: D
choices.text: f(x) approaches negative infinity

rationales.A: This chooses 100x^3 because it has the largest coefficient. Degree, not coefficient size, decides which term dominates. f(10) = 50,100 is still positive, but f(100) = -399,990,000, and the values keep getting more negative as x increases.
rationales.B: This treats the function like a rational function with growing denominator. f(100) = −399,990,000, and the magnitude keeps growing for larger x, so the values do not approach 0.
rationales.C: This reports the leading coefficient as if it were the limiting value. The leading term -5x^4 becomes arbitrarily large and negative as x increases; f(100) = -399,990,000, not about -5.
rationales.D: The term of highest degree, −5x^4, dominates for large x, and its coefficient is negative, so f(x) approaches negative infinity. For example, f(100) = 100,000,000 − 500,000,000 + 10,000 = −399,990,000.

stem: Let p(x) = (x + 1) / [(x + 1)²(x − 2)]. Which statement correctly describes the graph of p at x = −1 and at x = 2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hole at x = 2 and a vertical asymptote at x = −1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vertical asymptotes at both x = −1 and x = 2, and no hole

choices.label: C
choices.text: A vertical asymptote at x = 2 only, with no hole or asymptote at x = −1

choices.label: D
choices.text: A hole at x = −1 and a vertical asymptote at x = 2

rationales.A: Gets x = -1 right but x = 2 wrong. The factor (x - 2) appears only in the denominator and cancels with nothing, so x = 2 is a vertical asymptote, not a hole.
rationales.B: For x ≠ −1, canceling one factor of (x + 1) gives p(x) = 1/[(x + 1)(x − 2)]. The simplified denominator is still 0 at x = −1 and at x = 2, and the numerator is 1, so both are vertical asymptotes. There is no hole because a hole requires the factor to cancel completely.
rationales.C: This removes the entire (x + 1)² as if it cancelled with the single (x + 1) in the numerator. Only one factor cancels, leaving 1/[(x + 1)(x − 2)], which is undefined with a vertical asymptote at x = −1.
rationales.D: This assumes that canceling any common factor creates a hole. Only one of the two factors of (x + 1) in the denominator cancels; the remaining (x + 1) keeps the denominator zero at x = −1 in 1/[(x + 1)(x − 2)], so it is an asymptote.

stem: A function f is evaluated at equally spaced inputs x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, giving outputs 0, 1, 16, 81, 256, 625. What is the minimum degree of a polynomial that could model these outputs?

rationales.A: First differences: 1, 15, 65, 175, 369. Second: 14, 50, 110, 194. Third: 36, 60, 84. Fourth: 24, 24. The fourth differences are the first constant ones, so the minimum degree is 4.
rationales.B: Degree 5 is not needed. Any six points can be fit by some polynomial of degree at most 5, but the minimum degree is set by the first constant row of differences. Here the outputs equal x^4 and the fourth differences are already constant (24, 24), so degree 4 suffices.
rationales.C: 24 is the value of the constant fourth difference, not the degree. The degree equals the number of the difference level that is constant, which is 4.
rationales.D: The third differences are 36, 60, 84, which are not constant, so a cubic cannot fit. The constant differences first appear at the fourth level (24, 24).
